title: Constitutional Amendment A: Publication of Proposed Constitutional Amendments

context.text: Referred by the Utah Legislature as H.J.R. 10 (2025 General Session), which passed the House 70-0-5 and the Senate 29-0-0, the two-thirds votes the constitution requires. It takes effect January 1, 2027 if approved by a majority of those voting. A companion statute, H.B. 481 (2025), takes effect if voters approve (per KUER).
Ballotpedia lists two certified statewide measures in Utah for November 3, 2026.

question.text: Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers?

summary.text: Replaces the constitutional requirement that a proposed constitutional amendment be published for two months in at least one newspaper in every county where one is published with publication for 60 calendar days before the general election 'in a manner provided by statute.' The ballot explanation states that, if approved, state statute would require the Lieutenant Governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments and other Legislature-referred ballot questions on the Utah Public Notice Website and the Lieutenant Governor's website for 60 days before the election. Per Utah News Dispatch, a fiscal analysis in the state voter pamphlet says the change could reduce state costs by up to $1.4 million every two years.

measure.yesMeans: Changes the constitution so proposed amendments are published for 60 days in a manner set by state law (online, under the companion statute) instead of in newspapers.
measure.noMeans: Keeps the constitutional requirement that proposed amendments be published in newspapers in each county that has one.

argumentsFor.text: Republican Rep. Neil Walter, on PBS Utah's Hinckley Report (as reported by KUER), said newspapers are obsolete and the measure is about modernizing the system: "There has to be a new way to meet the requirement for notice and disclosure to residents," he said. "We're moving online, which is where people are."
Sponsors Rep. Anthony Loubet and Sen. Dan McCay wrote in the state voter guide: “Amendment A does not eliminate public notice. It updates how public notice is delivered.”
Loubet and McCay, in the same pamphlet argument: “By modernizing an outdated constitutional requirement, Utah can maintain transparency, improve accessibility and save taxpayer dollars.”

currentLaw.text: Article XXIII, Section 1 of the Utah Constitution now requires the Legislature to cause a proposed constitutional amendment to be published in at least one newspaper in every county of the state where a newspaper is published, for two months, before the general election.

fiscalImpact.text: Utah News Dispatch reports that, per a fiscal analysis in the state voter information pamphlet, if voters approve Amendment A and H.B. 481 takes effect, it could reduce state costs by up to $1.4 million every two years; the analysis notes the savings "would vary depending on the length of each proposed constitutional amendment and newspaper publication rates." The Salt Lake Tribune reports both 2026 constitutional amendments had to be published in newspapers at an estimated cost of $1.4 million.

supporters.text: Rep. Anthony Loubet and Sen. Dan McCay (both R), sponsors of the resolution, who wrote the argument in favor in the state voter information pamphlet.
Rep. Neil Walter (R), who defended the amendment on PBS Utah's Hinckley Report, per KUER.

researchNotes: The statewide ballot text is taken from the official county ballot published on the Utah Public Notice Website (the same statewide question appears on every county's ballot); the resolution text and legislative votes come from the Legislature's publication of the proposed amendments. The Lieutenant Governor's online voter information pamphlet carries the sponsors' argument, but the general pamphlet PDF available (vote.utah.gov) did not include the ballot-question pages, so the sponsors' argument and the fiscal analysis are taken from the Salt Lake Tribune and Utah News Dispatch, which quote the pamphlet. Utah News Dispatch reports that because the resolution passed unanimously, no argument against (or rebuttal) was printed in the pamphlet; no verbatim argument against by a named person or group was found, so none is listed (KUER reports Mary Weaver Bennett disagreed with Rep. Walter that newspapers are obsolete but does not state her position on the amendment, so she is not listed as an opponent; both the Salt Lake Tribune and Utah News Dispatch report no organized opposition). Ballotpedia is cited only for the count of certified statewide measures (two). A veto referendum on congressional boundaries, a public-union collective bargaining referendum and several initiatives are tracked by Ballotpedia as not on the ballot.
